title: Isomalt gems
subtitle: jewel-like sugar decorations made by casting hot isomalt into moulds
excerpt: Isomalt is a sugar substitute that melts cleanly, stays clear once set, and can be tinted with gel food colouring to look like coloured glass. It is the main material for hand-crafted sugar gems. The process is straightforward: melt the isomalt, add colour, pour into gem-shaped silicone moulds, and leave to set hard. The gems come out in about twenty minutes.
sourceNotes: Isomalt sugar-gem technique widely taught in UK sugar-craft courses from approximately 2010 onward. Isomalt melting and colouring guidance from professional sugar-craft practice.

glossaryTerms.definition: A sugar alcohol derived from beet sugar, used in sugar-craft for its ability to melt cleanly, stay clear when set, and resist crystallisation. It melts at around 160°C and is stable at room temperature.

content.text: look like precious stones and are used to decorate celebration cakes, cupcakes, and dessert plates. Unlike regular sugar, isomalt stays clear as it cools and does not crystallise at the surface, making it easy to get a smooth, glass-like finish.
Molten isomalt reaches around 160°C and will cause serious burns on contact with skin. Do not leave it unattended on the hob, never pour near children, and keep a bowl of cold water nearby.

Isomalt nibs or pre-coloured isomalt sticks, gel food colouring (if colouring your own), a small heavy-based saucepan, a silicone gem mould, and a heatproof jug for pouring. A digital thermometer is helpful but not essential.

Place 100 g of isomalt nibs in a dry, clean saucepan. Heat over a medium heat without stirring until the isomalt begins to melt at the edges, then stir gently to combine. Continue heating until fully liquid and clear, about 3 to 4 minutes.
If using a thermometer, the isomalt is ready when it reaches 160°C and is completely fluid with no cloudy patches.

Remove from the heat and let any bubbles settle for 30 seconds. Add one small drop of gel food colouring and stir briefly. Too much colouring muddies the colour; start with less than you think you need.
Pour the hot isomalt carefully into each cavity of the gem mould. Fill each to just below the top. Work quickly, as isomalt sets fast once off the heat.
Leave the mould flat on a work surface to cool for at least 20 minutes. Do not move it until the gems are fully set and cool to the touch.

Flex the silicone mould gently and pop each gem out. They should release cleanly. Store in an airtight container at room temperature; isomalt absorbs moisture from the air and will become sticky if left uncovered.

attrs.problem: Gems are cloudy rather than clear
attrs.avoid: Avoid introducing water at any stage; moisture clouds isomalt immediately.
attrs.fix: Ensure the pan, mould, and utensils are completely dry before use.

attrs.problem: Isomalt setting too fast to pour
attrs.avoid: Avoid large batches if working slowly; isomalt cools and sets within 2 to 3 minutes off the heat.
attrs.fix: Briefly return the pan to a very low heat to re-liquefy, stirring gently.

attrs.problem: Gems becoming sticky after a day or two
attrs.avoid: Avoid storing in a humid room or without a sealed container.
attrs.fix: Keep gems in a small airtight box with a silica gel sachet to absorb excess moisture.
